newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-BAD DAY FAILS TO HALT CORRETJA.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BAD DAY FAILS TO HALT CORRETJA.

text.p: Alex Corretja feared he was in for a bad day at the office the moment he awoke on Wednesday.

But, in fact, the Spaniard was simply required to put in a little overtime on his way to the French Open third round, surviving what he felt was his worst performance in a month and a half to complete a workmanlike 4-6 6-1 6-1 7-6 win over German qualifier Jens Knippschild.

"I wasn't sick, it was just one of those days when you go to the office and you don't feel like working," explained Corretja, the top-seeded Spaniard at number eight. "I woke up and I just didn't feel well and I came to the court accepting my game was not going to be so good.
"If I hadn't been mentally strong, when I lost the first set I wouldn't have recovered."
Corretja hasn't taken many days off this season, winning two tournaments, Estoril and the Italian Open, and reaching the finals in two others, Monte Carlo and Munich.
It is those results that have made Corretja one of the favourites to claim the grand slam event.
"I've said many times I do not feel any pressure," said Corretja, who crashed out in the second round last year losing to compatriot Felix Mantilla.
"I have had many matches on clay this season and have played well. It is the other players who should worry about playing me."
The 23-year-old is just one of half a dozen Spanish clay-courters seen as capable of walking away from Roland Garros with the title.
Corretja can expect plenty of company in the third round after 16 of the tightly-knit Spanish contingent, who often travel and train together as a group, won their first round matches.
The Spaniards' impressive start to the tournament has rekindled memories of the 1994 French Open when they occupied three of the four semifinal places and won both the men's and women's titles.
"We have said many times that Spain has many good players," said Corretja. "Maybe it is me this week and maybe next week it will be Mantilla or (Albert) Costa or someone else."

Corretja's rise up the world rankings to his current career high of number seven, has been steady but unspectacular, hard to distinguish from any number of proficient Spanish clay-courters patiently pounding away from the baseline.

Last year he made the finals of three tournaments and despite losing all three, twice to compatriots, he has forged a reputation as a tenacious competitor capable of beating anyone on his day, as demonstrated in 1995 when he defeated Thomas Muster, ending the Austrian's 40-match win streak on clay.

But Corretja is probably best known so far for his epic five-set battle with Pete Sampras in the quarter-finals of last year's U.S. Open, extending the world number one to the point where he was left vomiting on the court and barely able to stand.
